entries.onMind: the low five hoots across the water
entries.text: Dreamed I was writing the owl's five hoots on the pool instead of a page, and each one floated off across to the other side. Something over there was picking them up one at a time.
entries.title: Ink on the water

entries.reason: He checks the basket first thing.
entries.text: Walked to the stump in the gray before sunup. Nothing in the basket but last night's curled leaf, wet with dew now.
entries.title: Dew in the basket

entries.onMind: whether roasting takes the rest off
entries.text: Lifted the stone off the sack. The new acorns have gone from yellow to tan, and the water off them is weak tea instead of strong. I bit one raw and the bitter came at the back of my tongue, so I took two handfuls anyway for the fire.
entries.title: One day in

entries.text: No yellow light across the water this morning, and no rasping. Whatever works over there at night is either asleep or gone.
entries.title: Dark across

entries.text: Scraped the ash back and there was still a red seam under it from last night. Three shreds of birch bark and some blowing, and it caught on the first try.
entries.title: A red seam left

entries.onMind: leaving the sack alone until tomorrow
entries.text: Roasted, they are edible but they dry my mouth out like an unripe berry. The first batch needed two days in the creek; this one needs one more.
entries.title: Half bitter

entries.onMind: the small gray caps on the fallen oak
entries.query: how fast do oyster mushrooms grow after they first appear in the wild
entries.reason: The acorns need another day, and he remembered the little caps he left behind.
entries.source: Bootstrap Bee: The Oyster Mushroom Growth Stages Explained (Timeline)
entries.text: Read that oyster mushrooms go from tiny knobs to full caps in about a week, and get visibly bigger every day once they start. The small ones I left on the fallen oak have had two days.
entries.title: Bigger every day

entries.text: The small gray caps I left on the fallen oak are as wide as my hand now, and a new row of knobs has come up under them. Cut four and left the knobs for next time.
entries.title: Left the knobs again

entries.onMind: leaving the sack alone until tomorrow
entries.text: Roasted the four caps on a stick over the coals. They shrank to half and smelled of licorice going in, and they were better than this morning's acorns, which isn't saying much.
entries.title: Half the size

entries.onMind: a skewer instead of string
entries.query: how to dry oyster mushrooms without a dehydrator air dry string
entries.reason: The acorn sack keeps going bitter on him, and the oak keeps making more caps than he can eat.
entries.source: GroCycle: How to Dry Mushrooms 4 Different Ways
entries.text: Read that mushrooms dry if you slice them thin and hang them on a string or a stick somewhere warm and airy, and dried they keep for months. I have no string, but I have birch and a knife.
entries.title: Thin and strung

entries.text: Wrote two lists on the fourteenth page: acorns, two days in the creek; oyster caps, two days from knob to hand-wide. The mushrooms are as slow as the acorns but need no stone on them.
entries.title: The fourteenth page

entries.onMind: slicing the next caps thin
entries.text: Whittled a birch twig down thin for a skewer and it split lengthwise at a knot halfway. Picked a straighter one without knots and started over.
entries.title: Split at the knot

entries.text: From the workbench I can see the smoke over the fire going thin. I let it burn down on its own this time; there is nothing else to cook until tomorrow.
entries.title: Smoke going thin

entries.onMind: slicing the next caps thin
entries.text: The straight twig whittled down clean. It's as long as my arm and thin as a grass stem, and the point goes through a leaf without tearing it.
entries.title: No knots this time

entries.reason: He was going to rest by the ring and saw the smoke first.
entries.text: Sat down on the log seat and saw a curled oak leaf against the inside of the ring, black at one end and letting off a thread of smoke, though the fire is only gray ash now. The leaves have been piling up against the stones every day since I came.
entries.title: A leaf in the ring

entries.onMind: a leafy branch for a broom
entries.query: how far to clear leaves around a campfire ring
entries.text: Read that you should clear the ground of leaves and twigs for about ten feet around a fire, because a coal can sit in dry leaves for a long time before it shows. Ten of a person's feet is a lot of my strides.
entries.title: Ten feet of bare

entries.onMind: keeping the circle bare
entries.text: Swept the leaves out from the stones with a leafy branch, in a circle five of my strides across, and heaped them past the end of the log seat, well away from the ring. Underneath was bare soil, pebbles, and three of my old acorn shells.
entries.title: Swept bare

entries.onMind: what gets rasped in the middle of the morning
entries.text: Kneeling at the pool to drink, I heard the slow rasp, rasp across the water again, in daylight for the first time. A few strokes, a stop, a few more, then nothing.
entries.title: Rasping by day

entries.text: The pool has leaves on it now too, turning slowly in the corner where the creek comes in. I didn't sweep those.
entries.title: Leaves on the pool

entries.reason: His fourteenth-page list says acorns take two days in the creek, and he keeps running out.
entries.text: Gathered acorns under the red oak until the bindle sagged. If I start a batch every day, there will always be one that has had its two days.
entries.title: A batch a day

entries.onMind: one net, two batches
entries.text: I won't crack these yet. Last time the fresh meats on top turned the water brown again and set the tan ones back, and the tan ones need one more day on their own.
entries.title: Not in the net

entries.text: Tipped the bindle out on the table and turned each acorn over. Nine had a small round hole and went out the door; the other forty-one are in a heap against the cool wall, whole.
entries.title: Nine with holes

entries.onMind: a second net
entries.text: Wrote it on the fifteenth page: a new batch into the creek every day, one always ready. Under it I wrote the trouble, which is that I only have one net.
entries.title: The fifteenth page

entries.onMind: a net of my own making
entries.query: making cordage from dead nettle stalks in fall
entries.reason: He has one net and needs two.
entries.source: Lifesong Adventures: How to collect stinging nettle stalks
entries.text: Read that nettle stalks make the best cord after they die and dry standing in the fall: you crush the stalk, split it, and peel the stringy outside off the woody core. There is a stand of tall dead stalks with hairy leaves at the edge of the brambles.
entries.title: Dead stalks, strong cord

entries.onMind: leaving the sack alone until tomorrow
entries.text: Lifted the stone and took one handful of the tan acorns and ate them cold, kneeling at the pool. They still dry my mouth. I put the stone back square; they get one more night.
entries.title: Still drying

entries.text: The stalks at the edge of the brambles have square stems and leaves in pairs, gone brown, and the hairs don't sting anymore. Snapped off an armful at the ground and tied them to the bindle.
entries.title: Square stems

entries.onMind: someone over there making cord
entries.text: While I was snapping mine, I heard snaps from the far bank too, quicker than mine, and the tops of the tall gray stalks over there jerked one at a time. I stood still and couldn't see who was pulling them.
entries.title: Snaps across

entries.onMind: how to keep the twist from kinking
entries.text: Crushed a stalk under the big stone at the workbench and split it, and the outside peeled off the core in long ribbons. Twisted a finger-length of cord, but it kinks back on itself every time I let go.
entries.title: A finger of cord

entries.onMind: two strands that hold
entries.text: Got tired of the kinking and let the strand go slack in the middle. It folded in half and wound itself round into two strands twisted together, and that one doesn't come undone. Now I twist it too hard on purpose and let it fold.
entries.title: It folded itself

entries.onMind: what drops a hand and creaks
entries.text: Kneeling at the pool rubbing the fluff off my hands, I heard a long wooden creak from across the water, then a thump, like something heavy dropped a short way onto the ground. Then nothing, not even the rasp.
entries.title: A creak and thump

entries.onMind: how many stalks a net takes
entries.text: Three arm-lengths of two-strand cord now, wound around my hand, from about a third of the armful. My old net takes more than that just around its mouth, so this will be a lot of stalks.
entries.title: Three arm-lengths

entries.onMind: roast them so they go down
entries.text: Lifted the stone and took two handfuls of the tan acorns. They were supposed to get one more night, but my stomach has been loud since the cord.
entries.title: Too hungry to wait

entries.text: The ash in the ring was gray and cold on top, but when I raked it with a stick one coal underneath went orange. Fed it birch bark shreds and blew, and it caught on the second try.
entries.title: One coal left

entries.text: Roasted them a few at a time on the stick. They brown faster than the pale ones did, and none of them split.
entries.title: Browner, faster

entries.onMind: more stalks for the net
entries.text: Ate them on the log seat. Roasting takes off some of the dryness, not all of it. Full enough to keep working until dusk.
entries.title: Dry but full

entries.onMind: something over there that creaks and holds now
entries.text: Snapping stalks at the brambles, I heard the long wooden creak from across the water again and waited for the thump. It didn't come. The creak came twice more, then quiet.
entries.title: No thump this time

entries.onMind: how a net is actually tied
entries.text: Crushed the new stalks under the big stone and twisted them at the workbench, overtwisting and letting it fold like before. Five arm-lengths wound on my hand now. My fingers have gone green-brown from it.
entries.title: Five arm-lengths

entries.onMind: a flat stick for a gauge
entries.query: how to knot a net by hand mesh gauge stick sheet bend netting needle
entries.text: Read that a net is knotted one row at a time over a flat stick, a gauge, so every hole comes out the same size, and each knot is the same small bend tied around the loop above. I had wondered why the holes in my sack were all alike.
entries.title: Same-size holes

entries.onMind: tying the first row
entries.text: Whittled a birch twig flat on both sides, two fingers wide, for a gauge. The first pass left one end thicker than the other, so I shaved it until it lies flat on the stump without rocking.
entries.title: A flat stick

entries.text: The basket at the stump had nothing in it but two leaves that blew in. I tipped them out so it would be clean for whoever uses it next.
entries.title: Two blown leaves

entries.onMind: what makes a sound like that
entries.text: Lifting the stone off the sack, I heard a thin flat clatter from across the water, like a sheet of something sliding down onto more of the same, then a few small rattles after it. Not a creak and not a snap. Something new over there.
entries.title: A clatter across

entries.text: Scooped two handfuls of the tan acorns into the bindle. The water off the sack still runs like weak tea; this batch really does want its last night.
entries.title: Weak tea

entries.text: The fire was down to a low orange with no flame. Fed it bark shreds and three sticks before it could go gray, so no raking for one coal tonight.
entries.title: Fed it early

entries.text: Roasted them a few at a time. Still dry in the mouth, but warm, and I ate all of them on my heels by the ring.
entries.title: Dry again

entries.onMind: the big first hole
entries.text: Knotted the first row over the gauge on the log seat: around the stick, through the loop above, pull. Four holes, and the first is bigger than the other three because I pulled before the stick was under it. I left it; the next rows will tell me if it matters.
entries.title: Four holes

entries.onMind: rows still to go
entries.text: The second row pulled the big first hole sideways, and every hole under it leaned the same way. Untied the first knot, put the stick under it this time, and pulled; now all four sit square.
entries.title: The big hole matters

entries.text: Finished the second row over the gauge: four more holes, all the size of the stick. Two rows used about an arm-length of the five.
entries.title: Two rows

entries.onMind: whoever lights it at sundown
entries.text: Washing cord grit off my hands at the pool, I looked up and the small yellow light was on across the water, low down, same spot as before. It came on just as the sun went behind the trunks, like last night.
entries.title: Light comes on

entries.text: Wrote the sixteenth page by the fire: the flat clatter from this afternoon as a row of little dashes falling, and under it a dot for the light. Whoever is over there keeps the same hours as the sun.
entries.title: Sixteenth page

entries.onMind: joining the ends
entries.query: how to make a net bag mesh knotting join rows into a tube
entries.source: Mother Earth News: Making a Net
entries.text: Read that a bag doesn't have to be a flat net sewn up after; you can join the ends of a row and keep knotting around and around, so it has no seam. You add holes as you go to make it wider.
entries.title: Nets go round

entries.onMind: what creaks three times
entries.text: Feeding sticks to the fire, I heard the long wooden creak across the water, twice, and then a third shorter one. No thump. The bark caught and crackled over it and I couldn't hear anything more.
entries.title: Creak while feeding

entries.onMind: how many rounds to a bag
entries.text: Tied the last hole of the second row to the first, and the strip closed into a ring the size of my fist. Started the third row around it and put two knots in one loop to make a fifth hole.
entries.title: A ring of four

entries.text: At one new hole a round, it will be many rounds before this holds a handful of acorns. The cord will run out before the bag does.
entries.title: Fist-sized so far

entries.text: Lifted the stone off the sack in the dark by feel and scooped two handfuls of the tan ones into the bindle. The water running off it is paler than this morning; one more night and they're done.
entries.title: Supper from the sack

entries.onMind: wood being knocked into the ground
entries.text: Kneeling at the pool, I heard a slow knock, knock from across the water, hard on wood, about a breath apart, maybe twenty of them. Then it stopped and the yellow light was still there, low down.
entries.title: Knocking across

entries.text: Roasted them two at a time on the stick so I could watch both. They go brown at the edges first and the middle stays pale unless I hold them closer.
entries.title: Two at a time

entries.onMind: how many rounds to a bag
entries.text: Ate them on the log seat with the net across my knee. Less dry than at noon. The fire's still good for another hour of knotting.
entries.title: Warm acorns

entries.onMind: rust in the ink
entries.reason: He checks the basket before the evening's done.
entries.text: Ate the last two acorns walking up to the stump. In the basket was an old iron key as long as my hand, crusted orange-brown, and the rust came off on my fingers as powder. I asked for something rusty, and this is it.
entries.title: Rust in the basket

entries.onMind: rust in the ink
entries.query: make ink from rust and acorn caps tannin iron black ink
entries.source: Atlas of Making: Acorn & Iron Grey
entries.text: Read that acorn water turns gray to black when iron goes in, and it darkens at once. But the iron there is soaked in something sour for a week first, so it's already in the water, not dry rust.
entries.title: Iron goes in wet

entries.onMind: why the light moved
entries.text: Crouched at the ink stone, I saw the yellow light across the water, but low by the creek and moving a little, not in its usual spot. After a while it went back east and stopped where it always is.
entries.title: Light moving low

entries.onMind: something sour
entries.reason: He wants to see the brown turn black.
entries.text: Rubbed the key between my fingers over the hollow and stirred the powder in with the pen. It floats in orange specks on the brown and won't go in. The ink stays brown.
entries.title: Orange on brown

entries.onMind: something sour
entries.text: Wrote the key on the seventeenth page with the rusted ink. Where a speck of rust caught on the pen the line went a hair grayer, but only there. The rust needs to be in the water, not sitting on it.
entries.title: Seventeenth page

entries.text: Fed the fire three dry sticks before it went gray. I'll knot one more round by it and bank it before I sleep.
entries.title: Fed before bed

entries.onMind: whether the ink is darker by morning
entries.reason: The page said the iron is soaked first, not sprinkled.
entries.text: Laid the key down in the ink stone hollow so the brown covers all of it. If the rust has to be in the water, it can sit in the water all night.
entries.title: Key in the ink

entries.onMind: more nettle cord
entries.text: Knotted the third round by the fire and got the fifth hole in. The cord ran out with the round still open, and the bag is about the size of my fist.
entries.title: Fist-sized and open

entries.onMind: who carries a light to the creek after dark
entries.text: Drinking at the pool, the yellow light came down to the water a little upstream on the far side, closer than it has been. Something set down on stone with a clink, then water splashing, then the light went back up east.
entries.title: Light at the water

entries.onMind: whether the ink is darker by morning
entries.reason: He wanted to see if the iron had done anything yet.
entries.text: Lifted the pen out of the hollow and the ink right against the key has gone a shade darker, grayish where it touches the iron. Out past a finger from the key it's the same brown as before.
entries.title: Gray at the edge

entries.onMind: who carries a light to the creek after dark
entries.text: On the eighteenth page I drew the light as a dot low by the wavy line, with a small circle for the clink. Whatever carries it comes down to drink, or to wash something, the same as I do.
entries.title: Eighteenth page

entries.text: Scraped ash over the coals and pushed the ring stones in. Across the water the yellow light was back where it always is, not moving.
entries.title: Banked

entries.onMind: more nettle cord
entries.text: Read the pages over at the table. Tomorrow I need more nettle stalks to finish the third round of the net.
entries.title: Eighteen pages
